Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB369.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhe'an Fan. Zhe'an Jingfan owns the retained address, asking the fellow-monks of the two ranks to the hall: one embroidered garment is no fine sight; a single-stringed zither hardly stirs the ear — it takes those of the same breath seeking each other and the same voice answering, the honored bending to the humble, drumming wide the teaching's transformation, near and far made one, new and old both forgotten, inner and outer solemn, commands stern. Use Muzhou's heart-conduct to spur those beaten on the Hutuo; hold up Gao'an's bearing to scold Fojian's pickled greens. Beat Yangqi's drum, press Ciming's evening hall; let loose Xuedou's eloquence, entertain Taiyang's fine guest. Baoshou's raw ginger, sharp to the very last; Guishan's kitchen knife, free in killing and giving life. Even should a hero arrive, he will know this gate stands high — he may pick up a hint at most from the attendant's side. Thus can the true eye of heaven and humankind be widened, the hidden device of the buddhas and patriarchs broadcast, an unfading estate of the grove built, and the downward-rushing billows of the Long River stemmed. I dare pledge: King Shengyin never saw such a deed — how would the teacher Vairocana know this style of rule? Summoning the assembly: tell me — according to what is there such wonder?

Senses.Explanation: Free in killing and giving life — the master's own hand on both doors of the device, the stroke that ends and the stroke that revives. Feiyin Tongrong, charging the hall: the whole device unfolds — break chains with the iron-browed, crush bone with the exceptional-eyed, and that is why it is said: unobstructed across and athwart, free in killing and giving life, I am the king of the teaching, at ease in the teaching; the staff pressed on the knee: the Moye held crosswise, the full true command. Yinyuan Longqi, opening the summer session: our Linji cried out at the entering monk, Deshan took the rod — at Huangbo three askings, three beatings like wormwood brush; even now one more taste is longed for and no one dares strike — and when a monk offered, the rod was handed, and taken back with a blow as he reached. Look at this old fellow's working: like wind turning back into fire, like a galloping current crossing a blade — poison within poison, edge upon edge, teeth growing on teeth, horns growing on horns, free in killing and giving life, blazing through a thousand ages; whoever inherits the lineage must understand its purport. Wanru Tongwei, on what no device contains: nakedly clean, beyond taking up; always within activity, and within activity not gathered in — three mysteries and five positions, the black-and-white circle, six attributes and ten mysteries, none admitted; like night-pearl in the dish, slantwise beyond measuring; the Tai'e in the grip, free in killing and giving life. Ruibai Mingxue, writing to the scholar Yan from Bian Mountain: store deep and nurture full; when stray thoughts are exhausted and prajna is round and bright, then come forward — one rod, one stripe of scar; one palm, one handful of blood; free in killing and giving life, at ease in gathering and releasing — would that not be a joy! Zhe'an Jingfan, before the two ranks: beat Yangqi's drum, press Ciming's evening hall; Baoshou's raw ginger, sharp to the very last; Guishan's kitchen knife, free in killing and giving life — even a hero arriving may pick up a hint at most from the attendant's side; tell me, according to what is there such wonder?

Senses.Explanation: The concrete point at which a teacher works on people's behalf, asked after, shown, and denied in the records' own words. Fachang Yiyu asks the assembly whether Fachang has any such move at all and answers with the one pill that settles every illness, Foyan Qingyuan asks whether the mountain monk has one and warns that either answer would bury somebody, Yuanwu Keqin praises the heaped-up helping moves Xuedou spends on the first case, Yuanwu Keqin again, in the raised old-case collection, locates Mazu's helping move inside the illness-bed exchange, and Ying'an Tanhua offers to show the assembly his own by throwing the staff to the ground. Fushi Tongxian grants Qianfeng and Yunmen each a helping move and then rules both imperfect at second inspection, Juelang Daosheng asks whether stepping straight down from the seat leaves an intimate one, Baiyu Jingsi asks whether his dragon-flower raising has one and pays it out as a ballad, Zhe'an Jingfan sets Dongshan's three roads and Yunmen's one word aside, asking whether any helping move remains in his own Cao Shan summer, and Hansong Zhicao asks whether his greens-and-rice lodge keeps one and warns the assembly not to feed the rice into their nostrils.

Senses.Explanation: "To help someone, see it through; to kill, draw blood" uses a violent image to insist that a teaching intervention be complete. The named speakers use it for decisive instruction, reply, and case appraisal. Shiqi sets the line in a praise verse; Linye speaks it in a hall address and turns to a whisk demonstration. Jieweizhou invokes it in a Yunmen case appraisal; Zixian reports giving it as his own answer about Xinghua. Qianshan criticizes soft instruction; Qizong appraises Mazu and Baizhang; Liaozong applies it to freeing students from their bindings.

Senses.Explanation: For you, how many times have I gone down into the blue dragon’s cavern? Xuedou Chongxian’s verse describes repeated costly descents for the hearer, while Juelang Daosheng reuses the line as an answer about Dongshan’s further questioning. Xuedou’s line belongs to his verse on “sun-face buddha, moon-face buddha”; Yuanwu Keqin explains the descent as entering the dragon cave for its pearl. Juelang answers a question about Dongshan’s return to Yunyan with the same cavern line.

Senses.Note: The three-year-old child stands for the learner whom a teacher helps, while the teacher risks the two eyebrows by speaking. Shaweng uses the pair for the guest within the host; Dabian gives it in a question about precepts and concentration. Juelang answers a Chan and Pure Land comparison, Dabo responds to a question about the Buddha's awakening, and Tianyi uses it when challenged about his own speech. Each source is a different named teacher's direct response, not merely a repeat of an older case.

Senses.Explanation: Yunmen's warning line for all who drain their strength on the assembly, quoted, summoned, and shifted onto staves for six centuries. Yunmen Wenyan's own hall saying fixes the line — strain for the assembly and trouble leaks from the private gate — with the record's stand-in answer, all troubles already removed; Dachuan Puji summons anyone who will strain for the assembly this very morning; Liao'an Qingyu, fresh on the seat at Kaifu, grants the session is no different from Vulture Peak and asks the hall for the one who will strain; and Yulin Tongxiu credits yesterday's officers and chiefs, whose strained request brought the teaching seat, answering wherever people are met. Shitian Faxun, summing three old masters whose eyes differ while their innards match, grants that Vulture Peak cannot manage it but his staff strains for the assembly, raps it once, and steps down; Xuedou Chongxian, quoted in Wansong's case-three commentary, lifts a holeless iron hammer that strains and shoulders the burden well; Dabian Xianquan, at the Nirvana-day feast for the alms-collector, asks where the merit of the one who strains to repay the buddha's deep grace finally lands, answering with the eight-faced ringing stone; and Yunwai Xingze, after the Sansheng and Baoshou stand-out-monk case, finds no hand to shore up the gate, unseals his staff, and takes the strain himself.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Exert yourself for the assembly, and trouble comes through your own door
AlternateTargets: Spend all your strength for the community, and trouble lands at your own gate
SearchAliases: work hard for assembly trouble own door
Senses.Note: The saying points to the risk borne by someone who steps forward for an assembly. Masters use it both with sympathy and with criticism: an elder may work hard to help, yet the intervention can expose a flaw or draw trouble onto himself. The local case determines which edge is meant.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 縱然想得悟得，與汝了不相似。若要直截根源，只須於向來迷處下手，最第一也。有見說「煩惱即菩提，無明即佛性」等語，作任真無事會，五蘊本空會。功夫未盡，心魔未絕，任之斷之，皆成過患。有深信正宗，而自無智眼，不能甄別正邪，乍疑乍信者。或明解依稀，而不信自心圓具，成外取空者。斯皆信解偏枯，不遇明師，終成大病。有謂眾生與佛無殊，遂生增上慢見，見佛不拜，逢僧不禮，輕毀三寶，交結貴豪，甘投魔冒，教中所謂「飲醍醐而成毒」者是也。有專尚圓頓，尊重禪宗，遂指一切方便權巧之門為無益者。不知實因權立，權為實施。實既非實，權亦非權。塵毛剎土，處處菩提。法語妄言，悉是真實。何重何輕，皆是迷情妄生取捨耳。如上所宣，皆是打頭不遇作家，到底秖成骨董，欲昇反墜，求脫偏纏，是以不忍冷觀袖手，遂致緣古證今，入水拖泥，廣斥邪路，直示歸程。若問程而不行，與未問者何異？山僧今日偶然不惜眉毛，引起這般絡索，可謂開眼作夢，撒屎撒尿，不識好惡。若向衲僧面前，不過一場笑具耳。何以故？為眾竭力，禍出私門也。居士問：「經中謂不住相布施，功德最多。五度如盲，般若為導，色見聲求，是行邪道。和尚何故令人布施修福，念佛修行，而不直引入薩婆若海哉？」答曰：「布施修福等，何曾有分毫聲色到汝分上？汝自眼見空華耳。」居士不諭旨，再四請問。師曰：「般若能守護一切善法故，得入薩婆若。薩婆若者，即般若異名。五波羅密福德入般若中，即得清淨，清淨故得佛道，佛道即薩婆若也。《智度論》云：『一切法雖畢竟空，眾生顛倒深著，若不以方便力，則不可得度。』方便者，所謂六波羅密，相好光明，神通變化，能以一指動十方國土，梵音說法一切種智，大慈大悲等，具足無量諸法，然後能教化眾生，眾生必能信受。得如是力，假令妄語，人猶當信，何況實語？故經云：『雖知諸法實相，能人涅槃，但為眾生故，行檀等諸波羅密。』如經廣說，乃至不可以異事度眾生。又畢竟空中，諸波羅密無差別。若無般若，亦不能知是畢竟空得波羅密名。以入般若故無差別，如眾流入海故。世人不可但為說諸法實相，聞則迷悶，生於疑悔。故以第一義為心，用世俗語言為說，分別有諸波羅密，教化眾生。眾生實無有，法亦本空，不生不死，不退不起。色聲諸法亦然。又諸波羅等一切善法和合，能破煩惱、得菩提，而般若於中功力最大。以一切法自性無故，不取相故，

Senses.Explanation: Exert yourself for the assembly, and trouble comes through your own door names the risk of stepping forward for others. Baichi uses the saying in his own comment on an old exchange about slaughtering an ox. Poshan closes a demanding sermon with it. Yunwai gives it after admitting that his own extended instruction may make him a laughingstock. Huigong applies it to two old teachers whose accounts, he says, mislead hearers. Yikui uses it in a comment on Ananda urging the Buddha to speak. Lianfeng gives it while judging Nanchuan’s cat case, then asks who can save the remaining half.

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 禺中巳

Senses.Explanation: This fixed heading names the late-morning si period in a Chan twelve-hours song. Shishuang and Xueqiao use it as a turn in their respective songs; Zhaozhou, Tianyin, Lianfeng, and Xingkong each write a different stanza under the same time label, moving from hunger to practice in ordinary work. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 結跏

Senses.Explanation: Taking a seated posture (趺坐) means deliberately sitting down or taking the seat. In recorded hall scenes, Zhe'an Jingfan arranges his robe and sits before the white mallet; Huitang Zuxin takes the seat and raises the whisk; Wuzhun Shifan sits after offering incense and then speaks. The same words occur in death narration and figurative speech: Yongjue Yuanxian sits before writing his final line, while Jifei Ruyi says that he sits on his listeners’ tongues. The bare form (趺坐) does not itself state the fuller folded-leg construction explicitly written as “to sit with the legs crossed and folded” (結跏趺坐), or its contained form “cross-legged sitting” (跏趺坐); Sanshan Denglai’s verse preserves that longer wording.
